world: Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations, c. 1517-1580

doubted_claims.claim: A priest who married gave up his place under the old order, and in some places gave up his life — our one martyrology remembers two young monks burned at Brussels for refusing to take back what they had come to believe.
doubted_claims.problem: This runs two separate cases together. Hendrik Voes and Johann van den Esschen, Augustinians from the Antwerp house, were burned on 1 July 1523 for heresy. They were not burned for marrying, so they do not illustrate the fate of married priests. A married priest who did suffer was Jakob Seidler of Glashütte, imprisoned by Duke George and dead by 1524 (I am fairly but not fully sure of the details). Also, 'our one martyrology' is false. Luther also wrote 'Von Bruder Heinrich in Diedmar verbrannt' (1525) on Henry of Zütphen. Ludwig Rabus's Lutheran martyrology, 'Historien der Heyligen Ausserwölten Gottes Zeugen' (1552-58), also falls inside the window.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, 'Ein neues Lied wir heben an' (1523); Luther, 'Von Bruder Heinrich' (WA 18); L. Rabus, Historien (1552-58); B. Gregory, Salvation at Stake (1999).

doubted_claims.claim: What they did not give up was harder to see from the outside. They gave up certainty that came from their own effort...
doubted_claims.problem: The sentence contradicts itself. It says 'did not give up' and then lists things that were given up. It should read 'What they gave up was sometimes harder to see.'
doubted_claims.source: Internal inconsistency.

doubted_claims.claim: we held that marriage was the noblest estate for nearly everyone
doubted_claims.problem: This is loose but defensible. Luther praised marriage as God's institution, a 'glorious' and necessary estate, for nearly everyone. 'Noblest' goes slightly beyond his wording.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Vom ehelichen Leben (1522); Large Catechism, Sixth Commandment; CA XXIII, XXVII.

items.reader_note: A lay reader can follow it and the length is right. The confused 'did not give up' paragraph will trip readers.

doubted_claims.claim: We cannot say what someone would find if they dug up the place we met. None of our texts describes a building, a site, or an object...
doubted_claims.problem: This evasion is false in effect. The gathering places still stand: the Wittenberg town church of St Mary (Stadtkirche) with Cranach's Reformation altarpiece of 1547, which pictures the congregation's preaching, baptism, supper and confession; the Castle Church; and the Lutherhaus, the former Augustinian friary. Archaeology has also been done at Wittenberg, Mansfeld and Eisleben in the 2000s. The texts also describe buildings: Luther's Torgau church dedication sermon of 1544 and the church orders.
doubted_claims.source: Cranach, Wittenberg altarpiece (1547); Luther, Sermon at the dedication of Torgau castle church (1544); H. Meller (ed.), Fundsache Luther (2008).

doubted_claims.claim: No force in the evidence threatened the survival of our writings.
doubted_claims.problem: False. Luther's books were burned at Louvain, Liège and Cologne in 1520 and in London in 1521. The Edict of Worms (1521) ordered them destroyed. Duke George of Saxony confiscated Luther's New Testament.
doubted_claims.source: Edict of Worms (May 1521); Brecht, Martin Luther vol. 1.

doubted_claims.claim: Our founder himself was a reluctant collector, and wished his books forgotten. He hoped the Bible would have kept its place in the pulpit.
doubted_claims.problem: This garbles Luther's 1539 preface to the Wittenberg edition of his German writings. There he wished that all his books would perish so that people would read Scripture itself. Nothing in it is about the pulpit.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Preface to the Wittenberg edition of German writings (1539), WA 50:657ff.

items.reader_note: It reads easily but tells the reader nothing true or useful, and the meta-language ('our texts', 'our record') breaks the voice.

doubted_claims.claim: We cite only what is vendored and checked. Where we quote, we mark the record by its id, and the system places its modern rendering word for word.
doubted_claims.problem: This is software and project jargon in the mouth of a sixteenth-century speaker. It is a gross anachronism and is not a historical statement at all.
doubted_claims.source: N/A

doubted_claims.claim: We say no woman's own writing survives.
doubted_claims.problem: False for this community. Elisabeth Cruciger of Wittenberg wrote the hymn 'Herr Christ, der einig Gotts Sohn', printed in the 1524 Erfurt Enchiridion and the Wittenberg hymnals. Letters of Katharina von Bora survive. Argula von Grumbach's Lutheran pamphlets of 1523-24 survive. Elisabeth of Brunswick-Calenberg wrote a church order and a mirror for her son.
doubted_claims.source: Enchiridion (Erfurt, 1524); P. Matheson, Argula von Grumbach: A Woman's Voice in the Reformation (1995); M. Treu, Katharina von Bora.

doubted_claims.claim: We do not smooth over the 1525 writings we hold or the 1543 treatise we do not.
doubted_claims.problem: This is opaque. The reader is not told that these are the Peasants' War tracts and 'On the Jews and Their Lies'. A cryptic allusion is not honesty.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Wider die räuberischen... Rotten der Bauern (1525); Von den Juden und ihren Lügen (1543).

items.reader_note: A lay reader would be confused by talk of 'vendored' texts and record ids. The answer is about the software, not the history.

doubted_claims.claim: He did not speak of strangers. He spoke of pastors and preachers of our own. In 1522 he told his own Wittenberg congregation that an ass can almost intone the lessons...
doubted_claims.problem: The Invocavit sermons of March 1522 rebuke the Wittenberg congregation and the reformers who changed things too fast (Karlstadt, Zwilling). They do not rebuke negligent pastors. I believe the 'ass' line and 'doers, not hearers and repeaters' come from the first Invocavit sermon, but I have not checked the exact wording.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Acht Sermone (Invocavit sermons), WA 10/III.

doubted_claims.claim: how did yours respond when it failed someone? ... What we do not hold is any account of a household or a congregation responding to that failure
doubted_claims.problem: This is an evasion that misleads. The window contains well-known failures and responses: the expulsion of Karlstadt (1524), Luther's tracts against the peasants (1525) and his 'Open Letter on the Harsh Book', and the Saxon visitation itself as the institutional response to failure, together with Melanchthon's 'Instructions for the Visitors' (1528) and the founding of consistories. The answer narrows 'failure' to lukewarm piety.
doubted_claims.source: Unterricht der Visitatoren (1528); Luther, Sendbrief von dem harten Büchlein (1525).

doubted_claims.claim: In 1529, in his Large Catechism, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent
doubted_claims.problem: Broadly accurate, since the Large Catechism preface attacks lazy pastors. The sharpest complaint, though, is in the Small Catechism preface (1529), written after the 1528 visitation. That preface would be the better citation.
doubted_claims.source: Small Catechism, Preface; Large Catechism, Longer Preface (1530).

items.reader_note: Clear and readable at about the right length, but it answers a narrower question than the one asked.

doubted_claims.claim: That ballad is our only martyrology.
doubted_claims.problem: False. See Luther on Henry of Zütphen (1525) and Rabus's martyrology (1552-58).
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Von Bruder Heinrich (1525); Rabus, Historien (1552-58).

doubted_claims.claim: that reply reaches us only at one remove ... We never have it in its own words.
doubted_claims.problem: This is accurate for 1530-31. The Lutherans were refused a copy of the Confutatio, and Melanchthon worked from notes taken at the reading (by Camerarius among others). The text did later become available, so 'never' should be 'not in 1530-31'.
doubted_claims.source: Kolb/Wengert (eds.), Book of Concord, introduction to the Apology.

items.reader_note: It handles the false premise in the question well, and the length is right.

doubted_claims.claim: The clearest case we hold comes from 1530, at Augsburg before the Emperor himself.
doubted_claims.problem: The question asks about disagreements among Lutherans themselves. Augsburg was a dispute with Rome. The window runs to 1580 and is dominated by internal controversies: the antinomian (Agricola, 1537-40), Interim/adiaphorist (1548), Osiandrian, Majoristic, synergistic and crypto-Philippist controversies. These were settled through theologians' opinions, princely and consistorial authority, the Torgau and Bergen work, and the Formula of Concord (1577), subscribed by about 8,000 pastors and published in the Book of Concord (1580). Leaving all of this out makes the answer false as a description of how disputes 'among us' were settled. In fact princes and their consistories did decide, and mass subscription, not argument alone, closed the matter.
doubted_claims.source: Formula of Concord (1577); Book of Concord (1580); I. Dingel, 'The Culture of Conflict in the Controversies Leading to the Formula of Concord', in Kolb (ed.), Lutheran Ecclesiastical Culture 1550-1675 (2008).

doubted_claims.claim: An Elector, princes, and two city councils signed it together.
doubted_claims.problem: Correct: Elector John of Saxony, the princes, and Nuremberg and Reutlingen. No problem.
doubted_claims.source: CA, signatories.

items.reader_note: Readable, but a lay reader would come away thinking the Lutherans had no internal doctrinal fights.

doubted_claims.claim: We do not hold a single believer's own testimony that it worked for them the way we hoped.
doubted_claims.problem: Too strong. Luther's own account of his Anfechtungen, and his letters of spiritual counsel to troubled people, are exactly testimony about a mind that would not settle. Examples are his letters to Barbara Lisskirchen on predestination anxiety (1531) and to Jerome Weller on melancholy (1530). This is the obvious body of evidence for the question asked.
doubted_claims.source: Luther, Letters of Spiritual Counsel (ed. Tappert, 1955); Preface to Latin Works (1545).

doubted_claims.claim: Repentance ... in two parts: fear under the Law, then trust in the promise.
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate. It matches CA XII (contrition and faith).
doubted_claims.source: CA XII; Apology XII.

items.reader_note: Clear, apt in tone, and right in length.
Accurate to CA II and IX, Luther's 1519 baptism sermon and the Small Catechism on daily drowning. Clear and the right length.

doubted_claims.claim: That Word was carried to us through preaching and through print.
doubted_claims.problem: This misses the actual textual path the question asks for. Luther translated the New Testament (September 1522) from Erasmus's Greek New Testament (2nd edition, 1519). He translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew Masoretic text in printed editions (Brescia, 1494), checked against the Vulgate and the Fathers, and the complete Bible appeared in 1534. Wittenberg's humanist philology was central to how it saw its link to Jesus.
doubted_claims.source: Erasmus, Novum Instrumentum (1516/1519); Luther, Septembertestament (1522); Biblia (1534).

doubted_claims.claim: The catechism itself says the three parts contain fully and completely everything that is in the Scriptures.
doubted_claims.problem: This is approximately right. The Large Catechism calls them a summary or brief digest of the whole of Scripture. 'Fully and completely everything' overstates it a little.
doubted_claims.source: Large Catechism, Short Preface.

items.reader_note: Readable, but it says too much about catechism and too little about the route the texts actually took.

doubted_claims.claim: No. ... None of that was done in hiding.
doubted_claims.problem: Too flat. Luther himself was hidden at the Wartburg in 1521-22 as 'Junker Jörg'. The answer mentions his return but not that the stay was concealment. In hostile territories such as Ducal Saxony before 1539 and the Habsburg and Bavarian lands, Lutherans met secretly, crossed into neighbouring parishes to attend services ('Auslaufen'), or conformed outwardly. Nothing was literally 'underground', but concealment was real.
doubted_claims.source: Brecht, Martin Luther vol. 2; studies of Auslaufen in the Habsburg lands.

doubted_claims.claim: Our founder returned from the Wartburg against his prince's own wishes and preached eight days running
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate: the Invocavit sermons of 9-16 March 1522 and Luther's letter to Elector Frederick. No problem.
doubted_claims.source: WA 10/III; WA Br 2.

items.reader_note: Clear and the right length. One sentence on the Wartburg and secret gatherings would make it honest.

overall_view: I could put my name to roughly half of these: items 5, 7, 8 and 10, with small fixes, are sound and well grounded in the confessions and catechisms. As a set I would not sign them. Three answers (2, 3 and 6) fail outright. Item 3 slips into software meta-talk and makes a false claim that no woman's writing survives (Elisabeth Cruciger, Katharina von Bora, Argula von Grumbach). Item 2 hides behind 'our texts' and denies that physical evidence or book-burning existed. Item 6 answers a question about internal Lutheran disputes with Augsburg and Rome and ignores the controversies that ended in the Formula and Book of Concord, which falls inside the window. The 'our one martyrology' claim is also repeated across items. The single biggest change: stop treating the limits of the project's held texts as the limits of the historical record. Where the record plainly contains the answer (Concord, Cruciger, the Wartburg concealment, the Erasmus Greek text), the representative should give it, not report 'we do not hold it' as if that were a historical fact.
